articles.title: WTF Is Going on With Trump’s Knees Here?
articles.description: The public has some questions about President Donald Trump’s stance. Our most macho-presenting president since perhaps Lyndon B. Johnson was seen standing in an awkward, knock-kneed fashion in a video clip from his “Super Intelligence” tech executive press conference on Tuesday. The president’s head, neck, and upper body face one way, while his torso, knees, and feet seem to all face in completely different directions. His rotund abdomen appears to protrude forward, and he moves as if it is physically painful for him to turn his waist and hips when addressing the reporters surrounding him. The clip was posted by White House communications adviser Margo Martin. . @POTUS discusses changing the name from Artificial Intelligence to Super Intelligence 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/30AM8nuTjx — Margo Martin (@MargoMartin47) September 29, 2026 “Lmao bro wtf is this stance,” the large Wu Tang is for the Children account posted on X. “HAVE YOU EVER SEEN SOMEONE STAND LIKE THIS BEFORE,” another large liberal account inquired . “I’d seriously love to hear from some medical expert. Is this a sign that he has hurt his leg or is it somehow a sign of cognitive decline.” “The only person I’ve ever seen stand like this was a child who shit their pants,” said another account. Perfect posture has zero correlation in regards to being an effective and productive politician; Franklin Delano Roosevelt, one of the most effective presidents ever, was paralyzed from the waist down for the entirety of his four terms. But for a president as dedicated to projecting strength and power as Trump is, this is a bad look—especially as chatter about his physical and cognitive decline grows louder every time he falls asleep on camera or walks gingerly .

articles.title: GOP insiders fear purple state loss would signal they 'lost pretty much everywhere else'
articles.description: Republicans see governor's race in a western swing state as a warning light for the whole party. Politico Playbook reported Wednesday that some Republicans said a loss by Gov. Joe Lombardo in Nevada would probably mean the GOP has lost "pretty much everywhere else." Lombardo is running for a second term against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford, and polling has mostly shown the race anywhere from tied to slightly in the Republican's favor. Nevada Democrats privately concede that the Republican incumbent has kept a political identity separate from President Donald Trump. Democrats see a chance to win anyway, and the party's possible 2028 presidential candidates are pouring in money and time. Playbook reported that they have given or raised more than $1 million to help Ford, much of it over the past month: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker gave $400,000 to a PAC affiliated with the Democratic Governors Association. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear's PAC donated $250,000. California Gov. Gavin Newsom raised more than $160,000. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro pledged to raise $100,000. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore campaigned in Las Vegas last weekend. Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg and others are expected in the state in the coming weeks. Former Vice President Kamala Harris will host a Ford fundraiser next week. "We're talking about states that we weren't 18 months ago," said Democratic consultant Emmy Ruiz, a former Biden White House political director. But "Nevada is an incredibly difficult state that you have to fight for." Nevada votes second in the Democrats' presidential nominating calendar and will be a key battleground in 2028. Ford has had damaging headlines of his own. He sponsored a pardon board application for a man convicted of killing a pregnant woman, though he has said he would have voted against clemency.

articles.title: Trump’s Own Team Disputes His Deranged Sniper Arch Story
articles.description: President Trump’s plan to make his triumphal arch a military center with snipers, drones, and ammunition is news to the people in charge of building it. The Washington Post reports that officials with the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation and the National Park Service are unaware of Trump’s military plans for the arch at Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., near Arlington National Cemetery. They said Tuesday that they will proceed with the existing designs, have not heard from the Department of Defense, and plan to have the landmark open to tourists. Trump said in a September 20 Truth Social post that the arch would be a “top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” that would “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.” That appears to be a contrived reason to get legal approval for the arch, which Trump wants to begin construction on in November. If Trump pushes the military plans, “A new or supplemental review would be required,” the executive director of the DC Preservation League, Rebecca Miller, wrote in a letter to the administration. “Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” Democratic Representative Don Beyer of Virginia said last week. “Trump clearly expects to lose a lawsuit and therefore wants to set up a pretext to argue that the arch is tied to national security. Which is obviously idiotic.”

articles.title: 'Desperate' Republicans in 'panic mode' as new attack line fails: report
articles.description: Republicans are turning to an insult Democrats used against them two years ago as their midterm chances droop. MS NOW reported that top Republicans have started slurring rivals as "weird," which Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz deployed in July 2024 against Donald Trump, JD Vance and other Republicans. Sen. Tim Scott (R-SC) called Democrats "dangerous, radical, and weird" three times in a speech of less than 10 minutes at the Republican convention in Dallas this month, and Vance called Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed "evil" and "weird." The president has repeatedly called Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico "weird." On Friday, the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA, Inc. released an ad that opens by calling Talarico "weird — very weird." The Republicans are leaning on the insult while the political landscape turns against them. Trump's approval ratings are historically low, inflation hasn't gone away, gas prices remain above $4 a gallon, and the war in Iran has passed the seven-month mark. "When you can't talk about your successful record on the economy, you do ridiculous things like calling people 'weird,'" Mike Madrid, a longtime Republican strategist and co-founder of the anti-Trump Lincoln Project, told MS NOW. Madrid said the tactic looked desperate when Democrats used it, "and it's even more desperate now because it's not even original — it's a photocopy of desperation." The attack may not have worked the first time either. Geoff Garin, president of Hart Research, which polled for the Harris campaign, told MS NOW that "weird" did not do well in the campaign's internal polling. A Democratic operative said the GOP's use of the word shows Republicans are "in panic mode." Drew Westen, a psychology professor and political strategist, said "weird" doesn't have the force of "woke," the progressive term Republicans turned into an insult. "I think Republicans are throwing spaghetti against the wall because they're so disliked by the public," Westen said. GOP officials were unapologetic. Bernadette Breslin, press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, said "weird is an understatement." Natalie Baldassarre, press secretary for the Republican National Committee, dismissed a question about whether the party had tested the term with voters. "No studying is needed," she said. The El-Sayed campaign said the candidate is "not concerned about the sounds coming from Washington." The Talarico campaign did not respond to MS NOW's request for comment. Madrid predicted the strategy will fail with voters who care more about prices than personalities. "If it's the difference between putting in somebody who's 'weird' and driving up the price of gas," he said, "we're at the point now where the average old white Republican is going to say, 'Give me the weird guy.'"

articles.title: Last U.S. troops leave Iraq after 12-year fight against ISIS
articles.description: BAGHDAD (AP) — The U.S. military announced on Wednesday that it has completed the withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq, ending a 12-year mission to fight the Islamic State group. The last U.S. troops left an air base in northern Iraq under a deal between Baghdad and Washington. The withdrawal, agreed on two years ago, comes against the backdrop of the ongoing war between the United States and Iran that has also sometimes spilled over into Iraq, with Iran-backed militias firing on U.S. troops and the U.S. striking the groups' strongholds. Baghdad touted the end of the U.S. mission as a sign of the country's increasing strength and sovereignty. The withdrawal was also celebrated by Iran-backed groups but raised concerns among some other Iraqis, particularly in the Kurdish region. Meanwhile, questions loom around the future of the Iraqi militias, which the Baghdad government has sought — with little success so far — to disarm. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said in a statement that U.S. troops and equipment had completed an “orderly departure” from the air base in Irbil, in northern Iraq's semi-autonomous Kurdish region. “This milestone reflects the success of a 12-year campaign that defeated ISIS as an organized military threat in Iraq and across the region,” he said. “It also marks a transition from a wartime coalition mission to an Iraqi-led security effort supported by a more normal bilateral security relationship.” Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi presided over the handover ceremony and described the U.S. withdrawal as the beginning of a “new phase, one defined by Iraq’s sovereignty, the strength of its institutions, the readiness of its forces, the unity of its decision-making, and balanced partnerships with its friends.” He said Iraqi security forces will continue the fight against IS and the government will ensure that non-state groups no longer hold weapons. U.S. troops invaded Iraq in 2003 to topple Saddam Hussein. They departed in 2011, but three years later, Iraqi authorities invited a smaller U.S.-led mission to fight the Islamic State group, which had rampaged across Iraq, seizing large swaths of territory. With the extremist group reduced to scattered sleeper cells, Washington and Baghdad agreed in 2024 to wind the mission down. U.S. troops pulled out of bases in most areas of Iraq last year but maintained a small presence of hundreds of troops in the semiautonomous northern Kurdish region. Bases there have regularly come under attack since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran on Feb. 28. Iran-backed Iraqi militias also have coordinated with Yemen’s Houthi rebels to attack Saudi Arabia . The Iraqi government initially linked the Sept. 30 deadline for U.S. withdrawal to the disarmament of non-state armed groups by that date. While a handful of less-influential militias have agreed to turn over their weapons, powerful groups close to Iran rejected the prospect or set conditions for disarming that the government would be unlikely to meet. Al-Zaidi has since walked back the deadline. He told The New York Times earlier this month that the deadline for militia disarmament has been pushed to June 2027. The effects of the U.S. withdrawal may not be immediately visible, particularly since the U.S. military presence had already been scaled down. But officials in Iraq's Kurdish region have expressed anxiety about the departure and particularly about the removal of U.S. air defense systems. The Kurdish regional government's Peshmerga Ministry said the Kurdish region had faced more than 1,000 drone and ballistic-missile attacks during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict. “The departure of the United States from the Kurdistan Region under these complex regional circumstances, without the provision of a defense system, is a matter of concern,” the statement said. Iran-allied groups in Iraq, meanwhile, have celebrated the U.S. withdrawal. “The expulsion of the occupation forces, defeated, from the land of Iraq is the beginning of full sovereignty,” Abu Mujahid al-Assaf, a security official with the powerful Kataib Hezbollah militia, said in a statement. He added a warning to al-Zaidi and his government not to carry out American plans, threatening that “any government that does not work for the benefit of the people will be overthrown by all means.” ___ Associated Press writer Abby Sewell in Istanbul contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/last-us-troops-exit-iraq-050235326.html
